newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian September quarter GDP.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian September quarter GDP.

text.p: The average measure of Australian gross domestic product (GDP) for the September quarter rose 0.8 percent, to be 3.8 percent higher over the past year, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.
Economists' median forecast had been for a 0.9 percent quarterly rise and annual growth of 3.4 percent.
Of the three measures of GDP, income based GDP rose 1.2 percent in the quarter while expenditure based GDP rose 1.2 percent and production based grew by 0.5 percent.
A selection of economists immediate reactions to the data follows.
CHRIS CATON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST AUSTRALIA:

"Well, I think this shows that the problem with the Australian economy is not that it's about to stall, it's that it's essentially still stuck in second gear. 0.8 (percent) in the quarter and 3.8 (percent) in the past year does sound like relatively good numbers, but we know the economy is currently softer than that, we know that we'll be lucky to get a continuation of that growth in the December quarter."
CRAIG JAMES, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"We see growth in the domestic economy running at just under three percent at this time and as such not fast enough to make inroads into unemployment. One positive aspect out of the figures is the fall in the deflator of 0.4 percent to 1.3 percent annual. I don't think it (the GDP data) is really telling us too much about the economy. The partial indicators -- retail sales, building approvals -- are October figures where we are talking about September figures here. The economy is still flat, domestic demand is broadly flat looking at the June and September figures together. With inflation very well restrained and high real interest rates, there is overwhelming justification for a further
ANDREW TICEHURST, ECONOMIST, MACQUARIE BANK:

"Firm growth in the September quarter driven by private investment rather than consumption with deflators indicating that inflationary pressures remain subdued. In terms of implications for interest rates, it wouldn't alter our view that the probability of a further reduction in interest rates is slightly less than 50 percent."
NIGEL DOUGLAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, MERRILL LYNCH AUSTRALIA:

"It was generally in line with expectations, the one surprise being the fall in the deflator of minus 0.4 percent to give an annual figure of 1.3 percent. We had been looking for a number of about 1.5 annually so I suspect the negative quarterly number was a real surprise. That confirms the low inflation, moderate growth environment which we have been looking at previously."
BRUCE FREELAND, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"I think they're pretty much as expected. The general pattern coming through from the various components of GDP...all of that pretty much as expected, really indicating that the Australian economy has been going through a pretty soft patch through the middle part of 1996. The consumption growth of 0.3 percent again in line with relatively soft retail trade that we did see through the third quarter. To me the good bit of news, or the unexpected good news, was that the GDP deflator fell 0.4 (percent) in the September quarter."
BRUCE HOCKMAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:

"It is basically where things are expected although if you look at the six months we are clearly at the soft point in the economy now. I wouldn't be getting too excited about the GDP deflators, the domestic demand deflator is still in positive territory and not too out of step with the CPI numbers. It obviously makes the government's (business investment) forecast easy to achieve now with 3.8 percent in the first quarter. I don't think there are a lot (of policy implications) here."
BRAD HOLLAND, ECONOMIST J.P. MORGAN, AUSTRALIA

"It was fairly weak across most categories. Housing is still very weak, government spending has fallen off and company profits were quite weak. On the income side, wages were supporting it quiet a bit, but that really won't be around for long because we haven't had any employment growth for a while, and we don't look like getting very much. It's a fairly subdued picture and it would certainly accomodate a monetary policy easing."
AKIS HARALABOPOULOS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, GIO AUSTRALIA:

"Overall an encouraging set of numbers. These are not the sort of numbers analysts and the media should be hitting the panic button about. There are some onerous and worrying elements, principally a significant build up in non farm inventories particularly in the retailing sector. But there is a lot of good news there as well, productivity is still doing well, growth in the alternative measures of inflation is very subdued, household savings ratio has gone up, and the mix of growth looks okay. I do not think the Reserve Bank will budge (on interest rates) as a result of these figures ... They will more likely move, if they decide to move, about February."
